summary: After 4 iterations, the solution has achieved the maximum possible score of 100/100 on all 10 test cases and has been stable at this ceiling since iteration 2. The algorithm sorts a permutation using prefix-suffix swap operations, placing each element greedily in ≤2 operations, with a BFS-optimal endgame for the last 5 elements. The worst-case operation count is 1995 (well under the 4n=4000 budget), and average is 1986 across judge cases.
key_points: Score is 100/100 on all 10 test cases — this is the mathematical ceiling due to the checker's clamping formula: 100 * clamp((4n - ops)/(4n - best_ops), 0, 1) where best_ops = 2n+1 = 2001 and our worst case is 1995.

Iteration progression: iter-1 established the circular-buffer rotation algorithm (score 100, avg ~1990 ops), iter-2 added k=3 endgame (score 100, avg ~1989), iter-3 added k=4 endgame (score 100, avg 1987.3), iter-4 added k=5 endgame (score 100, avg 1986.0). Each iteration shaved 1-2 average ops while maintaining the score ceiling.

Further optimization (k=6 endgame via 12! BFS) is computationally intractable (~480M states, 2GB+ memory) and would yield at most ~1 fewer operation on average — with zero score impact since we're already at the ceiling.

Recommendation: STOP. The problem is solved at the maximum achievable score. All remaining improvements are purely academic (reducing operation counts that don't affect scoring). No additional iteration can increase the score beyond 100.
